question: An operations planner asks Claude to compress a six-week onboarding schedule into four weeks. The returned plan is detailed and internally consistent, and the planner circulates it as the new schedule. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The plan will be written for a reader who is far more senior than the planner is
B) The plan will take longer to read than the six-week schedule it is meant to replace
C) Claude will decline to shorten a schedule without seeing the original planning file
D) Steps were dropped or overlapped on assumptions the planner never stated or checked
correct_answers: D) Steps were dropped or overlapped on assumptions the planner never stated or checked
explanations: Register is easy to adjust and easy to notice. It does not determine whether the compressed schedule is workable.
A long plan is an inconvenience. An unexamined assumption inside it is what breaks the onboarding.
Claude will attempt the compression with whatever it is given; refusing for want of a file is not the failure mode here.
Correct. To fit six weeks into four, something had to give. Because the plan reads as coherent, the compromises it made are invisible, and nobody has confirmed that they are acceptable.
